name: Spot reduction exercises
lead: Spot reduction exercises are routines aimed at slimming one particular area, such as crunches for the stomach, thigh work for the legs, glute work for the hips, or facial and jaw exercises for the cheeks, in the hope that training an area leans out the fat stored there.[1][2] People use them to get a flatter midsection, trimmer thighs, a more defined jawline or a slimmer face.

The idea sits next to spot toning, which means building muscle in an area to change firmness and definition rather than to change the fat over it; muscle gained under a lean area can improve how it looks even when fat is lost across the whole body.[2] Where fat comes off first is described as strongly influenced by genetics, sex and hormones, with the lower abdomen, lower back and flanks often cited as slow to lean out.[1][2]

Wikipedia reports that physiologists and fitness professionals generally hold that fat loss occurs across the body with diet and exercise, and Grokipedia summarizes a 2022 meta-analysis that found no significant localized fat reduction, along with a small 2023 trial that suggested a possible exception.[1][2] Smaller studies continue to examine regional exercise, and some results are reported as complementary to general exercise.[3][4]

angle.text: People pick area-specific exercises, abs for the stomach or face and jaw work for the cheeks, to sharpen how that region looks. The visible payoff reported in sources comes through muscle development and overall leanness.

paras: Spot reduction contrasts with spot toning, which builds muscle in an area to change its firmness and definition rather than to remove overlying fat.[2] Where fat is stored and lost first is described as strongly influenced by genetics, sex and hormones.[1][2]

Wikipedia describes fat loss as a whole-body process: during exercise, hormones and enzymes mobilize fatty acids from stores throughout the body when energy balance is negative, and contraction of one muscle is not described as sending a signal that releases the fat directly above it.[1] Researchers cited there note that total body fat and its regional distribution are both strongly genetic, so people carry and lose fat in different places.[1]

Some depots are described as more metabolically active than others. For many people abdominal fat is reported to shrink more readily than fat on the lower body, a pattern that Wikipedia attributes to the activity of the depot rather than to abdominal muscle contractions.[1] This is one reason a visible waist change during a diet is sometimes credited to ab training.

The burning sensation during high-repetition work is explained in Wikipedia as lactic acid accumulating in working muscle during anaerobic effort, rather than as fat being oxidized in the neighboring tissue.[1] Practitioners often treat the burn as a sign that the area is being worked, which is how the sensation became linked to local fat loss in gym lore.

sections.h: Spot toning and how an area looks
paras: The appearance case for area-specific training rests on muscle rather than fat. Wikipedia notes that muscle development is easier to see in lean people, and that gaining muscle in both large and small groups raises energy needs, with fatty acids from stored fat helping to supply them.[1] Someone who adds abdominal, glute or shoulder muscle can therefore look more defined as overall body fat comes down, even though the fat itself is lost across the body.[1][2]

This is the chain most coaches describe: train the area for shape, change overall leanness through diet and general activity, and the two together change how the area appears. The tennis-player comparison of dominant and non-dominant forearms is a frequently cited illustration, since the trained arm was larger from muscle while skinfolds were similar between arms.[1]
Abdomen and waist: crunches, sit-ups, leg raises and ab machines are the best-known examples, and ab belts and electrical stimulation devices have been marketed for the midsection.[1][2]

Arms, thighs and glutes: high-repetition arm, inner-thigh and hip work is used with the goal of slimming those areas; in the studies described below, arm and leg training changed muscle size while fat change was generalized or small.[3][4]

Face and jaw: facial exercise routines are promoted for slimming the cheeks or sharpening the jawline. Grokipedia reports that these build muscle and that short-term changes may reflect water retention rather than facial fat.[2]

Grokipedia traces area-specific reducing exercises to early physical culture figures such as Eugen Sandow and to Bernarr Macfadden's magazines in the 1920s and 1930s, followed by post-war vibrating belts and reducing garments, then 1980s and 1990s workout videos, the ThighMaster and infomercial ab devices.[2] Social media, HIIT content and electrical muscle stimulation devices are cited as modern carriers of the idea.[2]

Grokipedia states that facial fat does not respond to targeted exercise and that facial exercises build muscle without reducing fat; it adds that lower water retention can make the face look slimmer in the short term.[2] Proponents of face and jaw exercises say that toning facial muscles changes contour.

On T Nation, one member logged a four-week experiment in spot reduction for the glutes using skinfold tracking, and another mentioned a study that suggested spot reduction might be possible while noting people jump on single studies.[5][6] A member also wrote about focusing on back extensions because his lower back was not as lean as he wanted.[7]

Studies described by Wikipedia and Grokipedia include a comparison of tennis players' arms, in which the dominant forearm was larger from muscle but skinfold measurements showed no difference in fat between arms.[1][2] In a 2011 randomized trial in the Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 24 sedentary adults did abdominal exercises five days a week for six weeks; abdominal subcutaneous fat did not decrease, though core endurance improved.[1]

A 2007 study of 104 adults did 12 weeks of supervised resistance training on the nondominant arm; skinfolds showed fat loss in the trained arm only in men, while MRI showed generalized subcutaneous fat loss with no difference between arms.[3] A 2025 randomized trial in 60 obese women compared general aerobic, regional aerobic and combined training for 12 weeks; general training produced more systemic fat loss, the combined group improved most, and the authors described regional work as complementary.[4]

Grokipedia lists further work: a 1984 sit-up study, and a 2022 meta-analysis of 13 studies (1,158 participants) finding no significant localized fat reduction, and describes a 2023 trial in 16 overweight men in which adding abdominal endurance work to running gave greater trunk fat loss, noting it was small and unreplicated.[2]

Wikipedia summarizes the overall research position as showing fat reduction that is systemic and driven by diet and regular exercise, with muscle growth in a region not reducing fat there.[1] Studies that report small local effects are generally small, short and not consistently replicated, and the 2025 trial's authors described regional work as complementary to general exercise.[2][4]
Grokipedia states that the US FDA has not cleared electrical muscle stimulation devices for spot fat loss and that the Federal Trade Commission has challenged misleading ab-belt claims.[2]

timeline.event: Bernarr Macfadden's magazines promote area-specific reducing exercises.[2]
Randomized trial finds six weeks of abdominal exercise improved core endurance without reducing abdominal subcutaneous fat.[1]
MRI study of upper-body resistance training finds generalized rather than local arm fat loss.[3]
Meta-analysis of 13 studies reports no significant localized fat reduction.[2]
Randomized trial in obese women compares general, regional and combined aerobic training.[4]

lore.intro: Spot reduction is a recurring topic in lifting forums, usually as a question of whether area-specific work changes local leanness.[5][6][8]

claims.claim: Training an area burns the fat sitting over it.
claims.believers: Proponents say working a muscle burns the fat above it, and the burn felt during training is often taken as evidence.[1] A T Nation member ran a trial on his own glutes using skinfolds.[5]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that the burning sensation comes from lactic acid rather than fat oxidation, and that the 2011 abdominal trial found no abdominal fat reduction; a 2007 MRI study found generalized loss.[1][3]

claims.claim: Facial exercises slim the face or jaw.
claims.believers: Practitioners say toning facial muscles slims and sharpens contour.
claims.experts: Grokipedia reports that facial exercises build muscle without reducing fat, and that short-term slimming can reflect reduced water retention.[2]

claims.claim: Adding core work to cardio may speed trunk fat loss.
claims.believers: Grokipedia presents a small 2023 trial in overweight men as a possible exception.[2]
claims.experts: Grokipedia describes it as small, male-only and not replicated; a 2025 trial in women found regional exercise complementary to general exercise.[2][4]

card.summary: Ab or face exercises meant to burn local fat; studies reported by reference works find fat loss is systemic.
card.aka: Spot fat loss, targeted fat loss
card.note: Mainstream sources report no significant localized fat loss; a small 2023 trial is the reported exception.

quick.overview:
Spot reduction is the idea that exercising one area, like the abs or the face, burns fat in that area. It is promoted in fitness media and looksmaxxing spaces.

Wikipedia calls it pseudoscience, and Grokipedia reports a 2022 meta-analysis of 13 studies with no significant local fat loss. Muscle building in an area can change its look.
quick.mechanism: Proponents think working a muscle draws on nearby fat. Researchers cited say fat is mobilised from the whole body according to overall energy balance, genetics and hormones.
quick.risks: Little direct harm is documented; the cited concern is misleading marketing, including ab-belt claims the FTC has challenged and EMS devices not FDA-cleared for fat loss.
